title: The Hann River
subtitle: A place guide to the spring-fed Hann River of south-east Cape York, which runs from the Great Dividing Range through Possum and Thaypan country into Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park.
summary: The Hann River rises in the Great Dividing Range on Cape York and runs about **140 km north-east**. It 'crosses the Peninsula Developmental Road and then enters the Rinyirru National Park where it forms a series of braided channels then re-forms to a single channel and discharges into the North Kennedy River' [ref:wp-hann], whose water goes on to **Princess Charlotte Bay** [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. It is a spring-fed sandy river, and its gauge at Sandy Creek has not recorded a single day without flow since 1968 [ref:bom-105001b] [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby]. The upper Hann is the **Possum People's** country and the middle and lower Hann are **Thaypan** country, both recognised by the Federal Court on 2 November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. **The Hann is not Kuku Yalanji country.** The Kuku Yalanji words across this site come from the Kuku Yalanji dictionary [ref:hershberger1982], not from the languages of the Hann. Both kinds of [crocodile](entry:crocodiles) live in this river system [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].

sections.heading: The river
sections.body:
The Hann rises in the Great Dividing Range and flows north-east for about 140 km, falling about 167 m on the way, from about 178 m at its source to about 11 m where it meets the North Kennedy. Its named tributaries include Jungle Creek and Sandy Creek on the left bank and Wangow Creek and Rocky Creek on the right. The upper catchment is on granite, there is sandstone in the Bathurst Range, and the floodplain is reddish-grey sandy loam on young alluvium [ref:wp-hann]. The river is named after William Hann, who explored this country in 1872; the prospector James Venture Mulligan gave it the name in 1875 [ref:wp-hann].

**Into Rinyirru.** Below the Peninsula Developmental Road the Hann enters **Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park**, spreads into braided channels, gathers itself into one channel again and joins the North Kennedy River [ref:wp-hann]. Rinyirru sits at the centre of the Laura Basin, 'a geological depression that drains northwards into Princess Charlotte Bay', and the park has '3 major rivers systems—the North Kennedy, Normanby and Morehead rivers' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The Hann is part of the Normanby catchment, about 14,837 km² in all [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby] [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby-catchment].

**Two crossings, two rivers.** The **Hann River roadhouse** is where the Peninsula Developmental Road crosses the Hann, at about 80 m above sea level [ref:exploroz-hann]. **Hann Crossing** in Rinyirru is a different place on a different river. It is named after William Hann because he crossed the **North Kennedy** there in September 1872 [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Anything said about 'Hann Crossing' is about the Kennedy, not the Hann.

sections.heading: Water: a river that does not stop
sections.body:
**The Hann does not stop.** The Bureau of Meteorology's gauge on the Hann River at Sandy Creek has run since 1968. In more than 20,000 days of record there is **not one day of zero flow**. The lowest daily mean was 0.037 m³ a second, in November 2010 [ref:bom-105001b].

**Why.** Springs feed it. In the Normanby catchment 'water seeps down through the high elevation sandstone and recharges the groundwater', and 'The larger springs in turn supply base flow to several streams including … Jungle Creek and the Hann River in the west' [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby]. So in the late dry the Hann is not dry sand with a chain of separate pools. It is a low, clear run of water joining its deep holes [ref:bom-105001b] [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby].

**Flood and low water.** The river runs highest in **February and March**, with a mean flow of about 20–22 m³ a second, and lowest from **September to November**, at about 0.3–0.4 m³ a second. The biggest daily mean on record was about 430 m³ a second, on 12 February 1974 [ref:bom-105001b]. Downstream in Rinyirru, 'During the peak of the wet season (December to March), heavy rains cause the rivers to flood'. The water spills out over the plains into billabongs, lagoons, swamps and lakes, and then dries back through the rest of the year. In the flood, animals 'disperse far and wide'; in the dry, wildlife gathers at the deep permanent [waterholes](entry:waterhole) [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture].

sections.heading: The year
sections.body:
The nearest long official weather record is from **Musgrave**, at 79 m [ref:bom-musgrave]. Musgrave Station is in Thaypan country [ref:fca-thaypan]. About **1,174 mm** of rain falls there in a year. January brings about 271 mm, February 295 mm and March 239 mm. By May it is down to 15 mm, and **June to September each average under 10 mm**. The storms come back with 14 mm in October, 59 mm in November and 182 mm in December. The mean maximum is 32.4 °C, peaking at **35.5 °C in November**, and the coldest month is July, with a mean minimum of 13.7 °C [ref:bom-musgrave].

**Wet and dry.** In Rinyirru, the rivers flood from December to March. 'Around April heavy rains ease… For the next 6 months the floodplains and associated wetlands dry out and by October the land is brown and parched' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Park roads close in the wet, usually from December to May [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013].

**How the Kuku Thaypan Elders read it.** Dr Tommy George and Dr George Musgrave, Kuku Thaypan Elders, timed their fires by signs in the country rather than by fixed dates. Gum tree country 'is ready for burning when the Ku akalmba Messmate is flowering', and 'The last of the light squally showers and the SE knock em down rain is an indicator… when Eriachne sp is setting seed and bark has shed'. When the seed stalks of the tall spear grass, *Kwern umbayal*, fall, it is time to get ready to burn [ref:standley2019]. The site's [seasons](entry:seasons) page is written from Kuku Yalanji sources; on the Hann, ask the Possum and Thaypan people how the year is read.

sections.heading: Country
sections.body:
Along the Hann grow 'stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark trees with a ground cover of coarse grasses such as speargrass' [ref:wp-hann]. Molloy red box (*Eucalyptus leptophleba*), *Ku ronga* in Kuku Thaypan, makes woodland on the floodplains of the Hann and the Morehead [ref:standley2019]. Queensland's vegetation mapping has kinds of country that match: a fringe of [paperbark](entry:paperbark) (*Melaleuca fluviatilis*, *M. leucadendra*), sometimes with [river red gum](entry:river-red-gum), along the major streams; Molloy box on the river levees of the Laura country; Darwin stringybark on the sandstone; and lakes and lagoons. These are types of country, not checked map polygons for the Hann [ref:qld-re]. The Atlas of Living Australia has records of the broad-leaved paperbark *M. viridiflora* (131), Darwin stringybark (105), Cooktown [ironwood](entry:ironwood) (50), river red gum (46) and Molloy red box (21) in the country around the middle Hann [ref:ala-hann-box].

**The Elders' nine country types.** The Kuku Thaypan Elders described nine kinds of country, each with its own fire [ref:standley2019]:

1. Messmate stringybark country, *Ku akalmba*, on sandstone and sand ridges.
2. Mixed-tree country: [bloodwood](entry:bloodwood), Cooktown ironwood and other trees on higher, light sandy soils.
3. 'Debil Debil' country, on stony soil.
4. Boxwood country, *Ku ronga*, on the floodplains and river terraces.
5. *Kwern* country: the open grassy plains.
6. Lagoons and swamps.
7. Gum tree country, *Ku garl*, with bloodwood, on the wetlands, rivers and plains.
8. Tea-tree country on sandy soils.
9. Wattle country: wattle and lancewood on the lower ridges.

**Fire.** Their burning was cool and careful. It is important 'to protect developing boxwood flowers through cool burns in the early dry season', because possums, insects, bats and birds feed on them. A cool fire 'that has burnt the dead grass around the yams' gives the [yams](entry:yam) room to spread. The old people called the brown falcon the fire bird: 'He picks up a burning stick from the fire, fly's away and drops it to make his own fire for hunting' [ref:standley2019]. See [firestick](entry:firestick), [hunting with fire](entry:hunting-with-fire) and [eagles and hawks](entry:eagles-and-hawks).

sections.heading: Animals and fish
sections.body:
**In the river.** Anglers surveyed in the fresh waters of Lakefield (now Rinyirru) from 1986 to 1991 caught [barramundi](entry:barramundi) and 'archerfish (Toxotes sp), tarpon (Megalops cyprinoides), sooty grunter (Therapon fuliginosus), sleepy cod (Oxyeleotris lineolatus), jewfish (Tandanus spp.), eels (Anguilla spp.) and long tom (Strongylura kreffti)', and fork-tailed [catfish](entry:catfish) were caught by nearly half the parties [ref:russell1993]. The sooty grunter is the site's [black bream](entry:black-bream), and the jewfish is the eel-tailed catfish. The Atlas adds rainbowfish, [spangled perch](entry:spangled-perch), the [mouth almighty](entry:mouth-almighty), [eels](entry:eels), freshwater prawns ([cherabin](entry:cherabin)), redclaw, [freshwater mussels](entry:mussels) and several kinds of [freshwater turtle](entry:freshwater-turtle) for the country around the middle Hann [ref:ala-hann-box].

**What the people of this country take.** The Court records that a Possum man described 'fishing for barra, jewfish, catties and spotties, and how he can find Cheribin and freshwater crayfish', and 'hunting pigs, kangaroos, goanna, porcupine, and plain turkeys' [ref:fca-possum]. A Thaypan man told the Court: 'We get wallaby, barramundi, freshwater fish and turtles and mussels. We also get bush foods like lady apples, white apples, bally yams that grow on a long stem, bush carrot and bush potato' [ref:fca-thaypan]. 'Porcupine' is the [echidna](entry:echidna) and 'plain turkey' is the [bustard](entry:bustard).

**On the plains and in the woodland.** In Rinyirru 'agile wallabies are abundant', Australian bustards walk the grasslands, and the waterbirds include 'brolgas, sarus cranes, black-necked storks, magpie geese and ducks' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The Kuku Thaypan Elders burned boxwood country to bring on green grass for the agile wallaby, *Nyeh myra* for the female [ref:standley2019]. Sugarbag, the native stingless bee with its hive and honey, is *Arear* [ref:standley2019]. The Atlas holds 99 records of agile wallabies, 164 of bustards, 164 of squatter pigeons, 428 of magpie geese and 462 of black-necked storks around the middle Hann [ref:ala-hann-box].

**Feral animals and weeds.** Feral pigs 'occur in large numbers' in Rinyirru and eat water-lily bulbs and turtle eggs [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]. Cane toads and rubber vine are in the Atlas records [ref:ala-hann-box].

**Not recorded here.** We found no Atlas records of saratoga, the Leichhardt tree, the platypus or the cassowary in the country around the middle Hann [ref:ala-hann-box]. The timber for Old Laura Homestead, in the south of Rinyirru, was pitsawn locally from Leichhardt trees [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The site's crocodile pages have the Hann in full: see [crocodiles](entry:crocodiles).

sections.heading: People of the Hann
sections.body:
**This is not Kuku Yalanji country.** The site was written from Kuku Yalanji sources, and the Kuku Yalanji words you will meet on its pages, such as [wawubaja](word:wawubaja) 'river', come from the Kuku Yalanji dictionary [ref:hershberger1982]. They are not the words of the people of the Hann.

**The upper Hann: the Possum People.** 'The Possum People's traditional country is agreed to include land and waters in south-east Cape York Peninsula, to the east of the Great Dividing Range', around the upper Hann and Kennedy rivers. 'It covers more than 375,000 hectares', and the group 'is made up of a number of clans, languages and dialects which include Freshwater Crayfish, Kangaroo-Rat, Tomahawk, Wind and Crow clans'. Native title is held by the **Possum Aboriginal Corporation** [ref:fca-possum].

**The middle and lower Hann: the Thaypan.** Thaypan country lies 'to the east of the Great Dividing Range, including Musgrave and Mary Valley Stations and the upper Morehead River. It covers more than 350,000 hectares', and its clans 'include Goose and Taipan Snake clans'. The waters of the determination include the Hann River. Native title is held by the **Awu-Laya Indigenous Corporation** [ref:fca-thaypan]. The language is Kuku Thaypan, also called Awu Alaya. Its last fluent speaker, Dr Tommy George, died in 2016 [ref:wp-thaypan-language], and there is no published dictionary. A Thaypan man told the Court: 'I speak in Awu Alaya language to the old people' [ref:fca-thaypan]. The Kuku Thaypan words on this page are from published sources and are given in italics: *Ku ronga* and *Arear* from the Elders' fire research [ref:standley2019], and *anharr* 'saltwater crocodile' and *awoya* 'freshwater crocodile' from the Hunter-Gatherer Language Database [ref:hgdb].

**Neighbours.** Kuku Warra country includes 'the town of Laura, Welcome Station, and parts of the Deighton River', and is held by the Kuku Warra Aboriginal Corporation. The Kuku Warra and Thaypan peoples made a Customary Rights and Permanent Arrangements Agreement on 20 July 2023 [ref:fca-kukuwarra]. All three determinations were made on the same day [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

**Rinyirru.** The park's Traditional Owners 'are the Lama Lama and Kuku Thaypan peoples', with their clans and related families, and the park is jointly managed by the Rinyirru Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland Government. The landscape 'features many occupation, ceremonial and story places' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture].

**Stories belong to their custodians.** This guide does not name or locate story places, and it does not retell stories. Walter Roth recorded stories from the Koko-warra of Princess Charlotte Bay around 1900 [ref:roth1903]. Ask the Traditional Owners, not this page.

sections.heading: History
sections.body:
**Deep time.** Quinkan Country, the rock-art country around Laura, went on the National Heritage List in 2018. 'Evidence of Aboriginal occupation is dated to 34,000 BP and rock art to 27,000 BP' [ref:quinkan-nhl].

**William Hann, 1872.** Hann led an expedition up Cape York Peninsula and found the Palmer goldfield. In September 1872 he crossed the North Kennedy and wrote: 'I came to a bar of sandstone grit stretching right across the river…here I crossed. The paths radiated in all directions, showing this to be a crossing place for the natives' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The country he crossed was already laid out by its owners' paths.

**Gold and cattle.** The Palmer rush followed, and miners used the track past what became Old Laura Homestead as their main way in to the goldfield. A lease for Laura Station was granted in 1879, and Lakefield and other runs later; by 1894 Laura carried 8,000 head of cattle. 'Aboriginal people contributed significantly to the early success of the cattle industry' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. See [cattle and horses](entry:cattle-and-horses).

**The park.** In 1966 the Lakefield Cattle Company bought Laura and Lakefield. In 1978 the Queensland Government bought both stations to make Lakefield National Park [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Today it is Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park, Cape York Peninsula Aboriginal Land, jointly managed with its Traditional Owners [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture].

**Native title.** On 2 November 2023 the Federal Court recognised the native title of the Possum, Thaypan and Kuku Warra peoples in consent determinations that are part of the Cape York United #1 claim [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan] [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

sections.heading: Crocodiles and staying safe
sections.body:
**Both crocodiles live in this river system.** Rinyirru is 'one of only 6 key areas for estuarine crocodile conservation in Queensland', and 'Freshwater crocodiles also occur here'. Crocodiles 'can occur in the rivers, creeks, swamps, wetlands, waterholes and along beaches' of the park [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe]. The [crocodiles](entry:crocodiles) page has the Hann in full, with the [freshwater](entry:freshwater-crocodile) and [saltwater crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile) pages.

1. **Treat every deep hole on the Hann as saltwater crocodile water**, in the wet and in the dry. No sign does not mean no crocodile [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].
2. Never swim where crocodiles may live. In the park it is illegal to swim or stand in water above knee height near a crocodile warning sign [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].
3. Fish from a few metres back from the edge, and never clean fish or leave scraps near the water or the camp [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].
4. Camp at least 50 m from the water's edge and 2 m above the high-water mark [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].
5. Take most care at night and in the breeding season, **September to April** [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].

**Old ways with crocodiles.** Around 1900 Walter Roth recorded that where people had to cross a 'known crocodile-infested river' on the lower Normanby without a canoe, a man crossed by diving, and that people diving for water-lily seed had a friend watching from the bank to splash the water if a crocodile came. 'The Princess Charlotte Bay Natives never consider it safe to swim even silently on the surface of these waters … when crocodiles are about' [ref:roth1910]. He wrote that big crocodiles were speared 'when stranded in the smaller water-holes after flood' [ref:roth1901], and on the upper Normanby boys played a crocodile game in the water, one swimming 'like the saurian he is supposed to represent' [ref:roth1902]. These are Roth's words, from his informants.

**Heat, snakes and distance.** November is the hottest month, with a mean maximum of 35.5 °C at Musgrave [ref:bom-musgrave]. Be alert for [snakes](entry:snakes); the park advises long trousers, closed shoes and a light at night [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe]. Coastal taipans and mulga snakes (king browns) are in the Atlas records [ref:ala-hann-box]. The park is remote, with no services and minimal facilities, and visitors must be prepared for breakdowns and for being stranded by wet weather [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].

sections.heading: Visiting
sections.body:
**Ask first.** The Hann runs through the Possum People's and the Thaypan people's country. A Possum man told the Court: 'I have rights to take resources without permission in my traditional areas… And people ask me permission for them to enter my country and take resources' [ref:fca-possum]. Before you fish, hunt, gather, cut wood or camp off the road, ask the Traditional Owners, through the Possum Aboriginal Corporation or the Awu-Laya Indigenous Corporation [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan], and ask the station too where the river runs through a lease. Native title holders taking food for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs do not need the licences and permits others need [ref:nta1993].

**Respect on the water.** A man connected to Kuku Warra country, around Laura, described his law: 'before I pull my line out if I'm fishing I'll sing out to the old people', and 'we must always leave three or four fish on the banks after we leave to show appreciation for the people of the country' [ref:fca-kukuwarra]. Of rock paintings he said: 'You can't put your hand on the painting on the wall – you can only look at it' [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

**In Rinyirru.** Camping permits are needed for every camping area and must be booked before you arrive. The park closes every wet season, from 1 December to 31 May for camping areas south of the Lakefield ranger base and to 30 June for those north of it, and roads can close after heavy rain. Domestic animals are not allowed, the tracks are not suitable for caravans, and the best time to visit is June to September [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].

**No spots here.** This guide names no fishing holes, hunting places, food-plant stands, caves or story places on the Hann, and gives no locations finer than 'the upper Hann' or 'Rinyirru'. If you find painted rock, stone tools, scarred trees or anything else made by people, leave it where it is. Queensland law makes it an offence to harm Aboriginal cultural heritage and gives everyone a duty of care [ref:acha2003].

groups.heading: In the river and its holes
groups.note: Fish caught in Rinyirru's fresh waters, fish and turtles named by Possum and Thaypan people, and Atlas records around the middle Hann. Both crocodiles live in this river system.

groups.heading: On the banks and lagoons
groups.note: The paperbark and river red gum fringe, and the waterbirds of the Rinyirru floodplain.

groups.heading: In the woodland and on the plains
groups.note: Stringybark, bloodwood, ironbark and Molloy box woodland, with speargrass plains: the Kuku Thaypan Elders' messmate, mixed-tree, boxwood, grassy-plain and wattle country.

groups.heading: Made and used
groups.note: Fire, fish traps and medicine from Kuku Thaypan, Thaypan and Kuku Warra sources; the rest described mostly from Roth's records around Princess Charlotte Bay, the Laura and the Palmer. Ask the Traditional Owners how they apply on the Hann.

groups.heading: Not recorded here
groups.note: No Atlas records around the middle Hann. Leichhardt trees grew near Old Laura in the south of Rinyirru.
